steps.text: Inequalities are everywhere in university analysis: when is a term of a sequence closer than \(\varepsilon\) to the limit? When is a function positive? There one rarely says "equal", but "less than". You learn the craft for this here.
steps.explanation:
Our roadmap:
1. Rules for inequalities – including the dangerous rule "a negative sign flips the sign"
2. Quadratic inequalities
3. Rational inequalities and case distinction
4. The absolute value and its rules
5. Absolute-value equations and inequalities
steps.insight: An inequality usually has infinitely many solutions. The result is therefore a set – written as an interval or a union of intervals.

steps.text: Inequalities are treated almost like equations – with one crucial exception: if you multiply or divide by a NEGATIVE number, the inequality sign flips.
steps.formula: a < b \ \Longrightarrow\ \begin{cases} a + c < b + c \\ a \cdot c < b \cdot c & (c > 0) \\ a \cdot c > b \cdot c & (c < 0) \end{cases}
steps.explanation:
The animation shows why: on the number line \(-2\) lies to the left of \(3\). Multiplying both by \(-1\) turns \(-2\) into \(2\) and \(3\) into \(-3\) – the order reverses. So \(-2 < 3\), but \(2 > -3\).

Adding and subtracting never changes the order. Multiplying by \(0\) is never allowed (\(a < b\) would become \(0 < 0\)).
steps.insight: Remember: multiply or divide by a negative number → flip the sign. Multiply or divide by a positive number → the sign stays.

steps.text: Linear inequalities are solved like linear equations. The solution set is given as an interval.
steps.explanation:
Check with numbers from both regions:
• \(x = 0\) (in \(L\)): \(3 - 0 = 3 \le 7\) ✓
• \(x = -3\) (not in \(L\)): \(3 + 6 = 9 \le 7\) ✗ – rightly excluded.

Double inequalities are solved in one go: \(-1 < 2x + 3 \le 7\) \(\;|-3\;\) gives \(-4 < 2x \le 4\), then \(|:2\): \(-2 < x \le 2\), so \(L = (-2, 2]\).
steps.insight: A check with one number inside and one outside the solution set catches almost all sign mistakes.

steps.text: Quadratic inequalities are solved via the roots. First solve the corresponding equation, then decide on which side of the roots the inequality holds.
steps.explanation:
Sign table for \((x + 2)(x - 3)\):

\(\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} & x < -2 & -2 < x < 3 & x > 3 \\ \hline x + 2 & - & + & + \\ x - 3 & - & - & + \\ \hline \text{product} & + & - & + \end{array}\)

The product is negative only between the roots. Equivalently: the upward-opening parabola \(y = x^2 - x - 6\) lies below the \(x\)-axis between its roots.

With \(\le\) the roots are included: \(L = [-2, 3]\).
steps.insight: Parabola opening upwards: \(< 0\) holds between the roots, \(> 0\) outside. For a downward-opening parabola it is the other way round.

steps.text: Particularly frequent and particularly error-prone: inequalities of the form \(x^2 > c\).
steps.explanation:
Taking the root turns \(x^2 > 4\) into \(|x| > 2\) – not into \(x > 2\)! Counter-check: \(x = -3\) satisfies \((-3)^2 = 9 > 4\) but is not in \(x > 2\).

A square is never negative, so \(x^2 < 0\) has no solution and \(x^2 \ge 0\) always holds.
steps.insight: Remember: \(x^2 > c\) with \(c > 0\) gives TWO regions, \(x^2 < c\) gives ONE interval between \(-\sqrt{c}\) and \(\sqrt{c}\).

steps.text: With inequalities that have the variable in the denominator you must not simply multiply by the denominator – its sign is unknown. There are two clean ways.
steps.explanation:
Way 1 – case distinction:
• Case \(x > 1\): denominator positive, sign stays. \(3 \ge x - 1 \Rightarrow x \le 4\). Together with \(x > 1\): \((1, 4]\).
• Case \(x < 1\): denominator negative, sign flips. \(3 \le x - 1 \Rightarrow x \ge 4\). That contradicts \(x < 1\): no solution.
So \(L = (1, 4]\).

Way 2 – everything on one side: \(\frac{3}{x - 1} - 1 = \frac{4 - x}{x - 1} \ge 0\). A fraction is \(\ge 0\) when numerator and denominator have the same sign (denominator \(\neq 0\)): again \((1, 4]\).

Check: \(x = 2\): \(3 \ge 1\) ✓. \(x = 0\): \(-3 \ge 1\) ✗.
steps.insight: Never multiply by a term whose sign is unknown. Either case distinction – or everything on one side and compare the signs of numerator and denominator.

steps.text: The absolute value of a number is its distance from \(0\) on the number line – hence never negative.
steps.formula: |x| = \begin{cases} x & x \ge 0 \\ -x & x < 0 \end{cases}, \qquad |a - b| = \text{distance between } a \text{ and } b
steps.explanation:
\(|5| = 5\), \(\;|-5| = 5\), \(\;|0| = 0\). Note: \(-x\) is positive for negative \(x\), which is why \(|x| \ge 0\) always.

The second interpretation is the most important: \(|x - 2|\) is the distance from \(x\) to \(2\). The animation shows that \(|x - 2| < 3\) means all numbers less than \(3\) away from \(2\): the interval \((-1, 5)\).
steps.insight: \(|x - a| < r \iff a - r < x < a + r\) (interval around \(a\)). \(|x - a| > r \iff x < a - r\) or \(x > a + r\) (outside).

steps.text: Rules for the absolute value – and a central inequality:
steps.explanation:
The last rule is called the triangle inequality: the path \(a + b\) is never longer than the sum of the individual paths.
Example: \(a = 3\), \(b = -5\): \(|3 - 5| = 2 \le 3 + 5 = 8\). Equality holds only if \(a\) and \(b\) have the same sign.

A consequence: \(\big||a| - |b|\big| \le |a - b|\).

Careful: \(|a + b| \neq |a| + |b|\) in general, and \(|-x| = |x|\), but \(|x - 3| \neq |x| - 3\).
steps.insight: The triangle inequality is the most important tool for estimating in analysis – you will meet it again in almost every convergence proof.

steps.text: Absolute-value equations are solved by case distinction: solve once for the case "content \(\ge 0\)" and once for "content \(< 0\)".
steps.explanation:
In the second case we get \(x = 1\), but that contradicts the case assumption \(x < -1\) – this solution is discarded.

So \(L = \{5\}\). Check: \(|5 + 1| = 6\) and \(2 \cdot 5 - 4 = 6\) ✓.

Simple special case: \(|2x - 1| = 5\) means \(2x - 1 = 5\) or \(2x - 1 = -5\), so \(x = 3\) or \(x = -2\).
steps.section: Chapter 5 · Absolute values in equations and inequalities
steps.insight: Every solution of a case must fit the case assumption. Otherwise it is only an extraneous solution.

steps.text: With two absolute values we need three cases – separated at the points where the absolute values "switch".
steps.section: Chapter 5 · Absolute values in equations and inequalities
steps.insight: Geometrically: \(|x - 1| + |x + 2|\) is the sum of the distances to \(1\) and to \(-2\). Between the two points it is constantly \(3\).

steps.text: A taste of analysis: absolute-value inequalities are the language of estimating. How close must \(x\) be to \(2\) for \(x^2\) to be close to \(4\)?
steps.explanation:
Step by step:
• From \(|x - 2| < 1\) we get \(1 < x < 3\), so \(3 < x + 2 < 5\) and hence \(|x + 2| < 5\).
• Since \(x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)\), it follows that \(|x^2 - 4| < 5\,|x - 2|\).

To achieve \(|x^2 - 4| < 0.01\), \(|x - 2| < 0.002\) suffices, since \(5 \cdot 0.002 = 0.01\). Exactly this kind of reasoning lies behind the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) criterion for continuity.
steps.section: Chapter 5 · Absolute values in equations and inequalities
steps.insight: Technique: split the absolute value of a product, bound one factor, make the other small. That is the basic pattern of almost all \(\varepsilon\) proofs.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips the inequality sign.

2. Solve linear inequalities like equations, give the solution as an interval.

3. Quadratic inequalities via roots and a sign table. \(x^2 > c\) gives two regions.

4. Rational inequalities: case distinction or everything on one side.

5. \(|x - a| < r\) is an interval around \(a\). Triangle inequality \(|a + b| \le |a| + |b|\).

6. Absolute-value equations: form cases, check solutions against the case assumption.
steps.insight: Congratulations! Inequalities and absolute values return immediately in "Sequences and Series" and "Limits": every convergence proof is an estimate with absolute values.
